summary:
Bolivia's 2016 Gender Identity Law grants legal recognition on the basis of self-declared identity through an administrative procedure, permitting a change of name and gender marker without surgery or a medical diagnosis. Gender identity is a protected ground in the country's anti-discrimination legislation.

The 2009 Constitution prohibits discrimination, and the US State Department's 2011 Human Rights Report on Bolivia documented that constitutional guarantee alongside persistent societal discrimination against LGBT people.

The 2016 statute was enacted despite low public support for trans rights. Trans activists secured access to legislators of the ruling party, and heteronormative provisions were adopted in the same period because organised religion and LGBT organisations were both constituencies of the party in government. Contradictory laws therefore stand side by side, so a visitor who relies on the gender-identity statute may still encounter provisions built on a heterosexual, cisgender presumption.

Partner recognition followed later: the Inter-American Court of Human Rights issued an opinion in January 2018, and in December 2020 Bolivia's civil registry recognised free unions between same-sex couples.

Formal protection has not produced equal treatment in practice. Agencia Presentes reported in December 2024 that Bolivia's first virtual survey of LGBTI people documented what it called the great exclusion of LGBTI people in the country.

Official institutions show the same gap. Reporting from August 2014 described homosexuality as taboo in Bolivia's armed forces, with gay soldiers testifying anonymously to discrimination and sanctions.
tangentialFactors:
The constitutional framework frames protection in gendered terms: Article 15(II) addresses violence, Article 45(V) guarantees protection of maternity, and Title VIII of the Penal Code governs abortion. These provisions do not speak to trans identity directly but shape the statutory environment a trans person enters.

The January 2018 Inter-American Court of Human Rights opinion situates Bolivia within a regional legal conversation on gender identity and same-sex union, and the December 2020 civil-registry recognition of free unions aligns Bolivian family law with that regional movement.

The legislative politics behind the 2016 law are documented in a Comparative Politics article of April 2024, which attributes the statute to trans activists' access to ruling-party legislators rather than to majority public opinion, and which records that organised religion and LGBT activists were competing constituencies of the same party.

Advocacy for openness in the armed forces has been carried by the TLGB collective and by human-rights activists, whose demands were voiced alongside the anonymous testimony of gay soldiers in 2014.
localsOnly:
Residents obtain legal recognition through an administrative process on the basis of self-declared identity, with no surgical or diagnostic prerequisite, and gender identity is a protected ground when challenging discrimination.

Residents live with documented exclusion notwithstanding the statute: the first virtual survey of LGBTI people in the country, published in December 2024, found extensive exclusion of LGBTI people in Bolivia.

Same-sex couples have had free unions recognised by the civil registry since December 2020, giving residents a route to partner recognition that is not available to unmarried couples in every respect.

Service members face a different regime: gay soldiers reported discrimination and sanctions in the armed forces, and the TLGB collective and human-rights activists have demanded openness in that institution.
outOfScopeNotes:
The inventory contains no sourced material on entry or visa rules for trans travellers, on airport or border screening that could disclose gender history, on which gender markers Bolivian authorities accept in foreign passports, on bathroom or facility access rules, on hate-crime sentencing, or on access to legal and medical care while visiting. Those questions remain unresolved on this record.

Whether the administrative recognition process under the 2016 law is available to non-residents or holders of foreign documents is not stated in any source here.

Whether the discrimination documented in Bolivia's armed forces in 2014 persists in its 2014 form is not sourced by the inventory; the reporting is dated and its current status unresolved.

The December 2024 survey source does not give its sample size, method, or whether trans respondents were identified separately from LGBTI respondents as a whole, so the strength of that finding cannot be assessed from this inventory.

A Newsweek article of July 2017 counting 18 countries believed to fully legalise LGBT military service after the US trans military ban does not single out Bolivia and cannot be used to characterise Bolivian policy.

The US State Department's 2011 report also covers arbitrary deprivation of life, prison conditions and corruption; that material is outside the scope of trans visitor risk and has not been carried into the record.
